en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to the glorious gurus.
The Cluster of the Essence of Non-Duality (Advaitarasamañjarī)
How could I perform a hymn of praise or similar acts for the Self, which is the undivided nectar of truth, knowledge, and bliss, since It is beyond the reach of the senses? || 1 ||
She who, out of a desire solely to protect her own devotees, shines forth pervading all the worlds;
she who, in the form of the vowels beginning with 'a', is praised by Śuka and others.
I bow to that Śrī Lalitā, my own chosen deity. || 2 ||
Having assumed an elephantine face above and a human body below to demonstrate the supreme unity of the two,
he shines forth beyond the net of delusion as the Great One.
Therefore, let there be here before me that which is most excellent among things. || 3 ||
Near the banyan tree, he who dwells in the form of Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti for the sake of the welfare of all, with his auspicious seal of Being-Consciousness (saccinmudrā),
in order to bestow the supreme nectar upon his disciples—
Therefore, I meditate here upon that one supreme bestower of boons, who is empty of intrinsic being. || 4 ||
Meditating upon the circle of the lords of ascetics, who are themselves a circle of unbroken aesthetic essence,
may he cause the jasmine flower of the nectar of non-duality to bloom beautifully today.
Though unbound, this [state] is well-bound for the virtuous one who possesses excellent vision;
for the virtuous, possessing contentment, remain peaceful through their even-sightedness.
For me, who am like a bird flying through the void of the quarters, the state of being the Sun is indeed exceedingly difficult to attain;
yet may those of friendly heart forgive the audacity of one who, though knowing this, still desires to achieve it.
Non-duality alone is the ultimate reality; it is that which has assumed the form and configuration of both an elephant and a man for the sake of discernment,
and it is the flawless object of knowledge for those who know all things.
May the boon-granting King of Obstacles reveal it to me. || 1 ||
For one who relies on ignorance, wherein the manifold distinctions of the self flash forth from that very ignorance, liberation is not easily attained;
it is like [seeking] an infinite reflection within the interior of a mirror-house.
For the child who has gone to the door, there is no exit once he has gone outside.
One who possesses the means for pacification and other rites attains his own state through the words of the excellent teacher,
just as a man led by thieves to the bank of a river reaches it himself.
For one's own country is indeed accessible only through the speech of those who know it. || 3 ||
Through the words of the Guru’s Upanishads,
"You are the Infinite," the notion of being a limited agent dissolves and the state of infinity is realized,
just as a prince realizes his true nature upon being informed of it.
The state of being a king [arises] as if from the dissolving away of the nature of disease. || 4 ||
The notion that there can be bondage or liberation for the inner self, whose body is immutable, eternal bliss, and consciousness, is a delusion and a perverse fancy—
like describing the physical form or the qualities of the son of a barren woman.
Thus, even this state of being fivefold is merely a conceptual construction.
At first glance, the doctrine that the world exists appears formidable;
yet in truth, when subjected to analytical investigation, nothing at all exists.
To the fearful, darkness appears on all sides as if it were a demon.
Is there anything else that can be brought right there, such as the flame of a lamp? || 6 ||

When investigated, it is consciousness alone that shines as the self of the world; there is no other entity whatsoever. It is like the rope, which is the substratum of the delusion, being more real than the illusory snake.
Could it possibly be another reality in any way whatsoever? || 7 ||
Even this entire universe is merely an illusion;
being the Self alone, it is the manifestation of bliss that is not other than itself.
If it is argued that the universe is said to be real simply because of its manifestation, [then...]
Who indeed could become wealthy through silver in a mother-of-pearl shell? || 8 ||
It does not exist at the moment of its dependence, nor before, nor after;
nevertheless, this entire universe appears. Or rather, what is more wonderful than this? Is it not a great magical illusion?
For it appears as something conceptualized through illusion. || 9 ||
Though he is one, this Infinite One appears as many due to his association with the veil of darkness imagined by himself;
even though the moon is devoid of a second, it appears to have a companion.
It appears as such due to the person's own defect of the sense organ. || 10 ||
The wheel of the world is perceived as a whirling firebrand,
an expansion of extreme delusion and instability; yet,
by fate, when the cessation of this wandering is about to arrive, it is brought to an end.
Indeed, that very same thing is not seen again as it was before.
This world is a city of Gandharvas, unstable, shining for us in the sky named consciousness;
and if the knowledge of the Self flashes forth, it is like a flash of lightning.
At that very moment, all of this immediately vanishes.
By dissolving the world that has been superposed,
our mind remains as the nature of Śiva;
just as when enemies have been slain, the slayer remains standing after they have fallen below.
He becomes a scent-elephant, entirely without a second. || 13 ||
Let the body that consumes food go to its destruction this very day;
even so, what difference does that make for me, whose nature is consciousness?
Whether the jar perishes now or remains for a long time, it makes no distinction to me.
In the sky of the pot, there is not even a trace of distinction. || 14 ||
With dull intellect, he was deluded into thinking that the entire universe— whose forms are imagined through mere conceptualization— is real; yet,
having recognized the woman produced by the intensity of his thought, he understood her to be such.
He leaps about like one long separated [from his beloved], crying out, "O Śiva! || 15 ||
That which, due to delusion, is designated as "the world" within me— my own self, which is the realization of the bliss of truth through its own inherent nature—
is seen nowhere else and is formless, yet appears to have form.
We conclude that this is a picture of the headless trunk. || 16 ||
The essence of consciousness never abandons its state of being a single flavor, even though it is concealed by the distinctions of superimposed manifestations; nor does it lose its unity,
even when variegated by the diverse array of various moving and non-moving beings.
A variegated cloth does not abandon its own nature as cloth.
If someone were to consider with absolute certainty that "I am" the reality of the Self— which is conscious, blissful in nature, and indivisible—
then even the body and senses would be [seen as such] through the latent impressions of delusion.
Just as the self of the ignorant is pervaded by the notions of "mine" and "I. || 18 ||
Having ascertained that the universe is false and devoid of essence, the sages taste within themselves that inner essence which is the nature of rasa,
having cast aside the essence of the mirage-born heat born of suffering.
It is resorted to by those of noble intellect, like the full tide of the ocean of the gods.
Alas, people of deluded intellect do not respect such a reality of the Self, which is ever-present and close at hand;
it is the very domain of space that illumines the entire world.
Owls do not venture to gaze upon the sun.
The deluded person, having conceptualized the manifold world— which is in essence a vibration of bliss— as something other, falls into distress;
[yet he fails to see] the manifestation of his own body within lamps and such.
Having plunged into a shadow, does a fool not become utterly bewildered? || 21 ||
Māyā is not able to alter the Self— which is unattached— by means of its own networks of transformations such as space and so forth;
it is like a torrent of water falling upon the surface of a lotus leaf that serves as its support.
Why should he moisten [them] with his own showers of spray? || 22 ||
The conceptual constructions of the world, whose bodies consist of mere appearances,
do not touch me, who am liberated from all attachments;
nor do the various attributes such as impurity, which are superimposed [upon reality].
Why indeed do they moisten the stainless expanse of the sky? || 23 ||
The three states— dream, deep sleep, and waking— are indeed constantly subject to rising and setting,
like the rows of sloughed skins upon the body of a great serpent king.
They shine forth while I alone remain as the witnessing subject.
The distinction made by the words "dream" and "waking" is merely verbal;
the illusory nature (*māyāmayatva*) of both is exactly the same. The conceptual differentiation based on the names "inner" (*pratyak*) and "outer" (*parāk*) is likewise nominal.
But the nature of those two is the bliss of the realization of truth. || 25 ||
With all sensory faculties stilled and the conceptual constructions of the world pacified,
they experience the state of deep sleep even while awake, in which the realization of the *caitya* remains as nothing but their own innate bliss.
Those who constantly sport within themselves in the realization of Truth. || 26 ||
If those who observe my physical movements perceive me as the "doer," what of it? Whether I am thus perceived or not, I remain exactly as I am.
This notion that "this one is wavering" is merely grasped by the intellect of the vulgar.
The moon is not likewise [reflected] when it is in proximity to a moving cloud. || 27 ||
Let the world’s manifold variety indeed manifest falsely; even so, there is no loss for one who knows the stainless reality,
just as there is no harm when seeing terrifying elephants and such in a dream.
For one who does not reflect upon the dream-like nature [of things], there is no fear. || 28 ||

Even though one has determined that this world is absolutely non-existent and lacks any fixed order, the perception of a self within me still persists; for even one who has resolved that "there is no face here" [is immediately overcome by doubt].
He indeed took up a mirror for the purpose of beholding his face. || 29 ||
Though awakened at every morsel by his mother, like a child drowsy with sleep and unaware of anything else,
he perceives even as he looks upon the external world as a magical illusion.
I have not fallen away from my mantra by even a single fraction. || 30 ||
When the visible world becomes manifest, the plenitude (bhūman) is not seen at all; when the plenitude becomes manifest, the visible world is not seen at all.
Just as this earth is not perceived when another continent is flashing before one's eyes.
It vibrates upon the circle of the earth, yet it is not seen as such.
As awakening gradually attains growth, even that stainless delusion is severed within the heart,
just as the moon increases day by day with its digits.
Just as even a great darkness becomes dimmed. ||32||
When the Lord of Sages is filled with the essence of the experience of Brahman, the methods for the continuity of karma turn away from him;
he is satiated by drinking the elixir pointed out by the Siddhas.
Do injunctions indeed operate with reference to an object that has already been accomplished? 33.

Although the Sage had attained the state of being the self of all, he maintained his former meditative absorption in order to fulfill his commitment; likewise, although the king possessed every abundance, he waited for the proper time.
For the sake of leading [beings] to liberation, he enjoys the play of the four limbs. || 34 ||
The prohibitions favored by the Vedas bring joy to the knower of the Self, for whom all ritual activities have ceased,
who is indifferent to all mere activity, and who is profoundly tranquil.
These charming [verses] are composed in the Māśabdaka style. || 35 ||
The sovereign of sages, intent on contemplating reality,
is not to be questioned even while acting according to his own will;
for having attained sovereignty, he may conduct himself as he pleases.
A king can certainly not be questioned by his subjects. || 36 ||
A person attains purification only while experiencing the misfortunes or the abundant prosperity born of past karma;
or is it like a serpent whose body has been seized by a snake-charmer?
He is able to avoid the established rules for punishment. || 37 ||

One who perceives the ultimate truth would not experience the abundance or misfortune resulting from the virtuous and non-virtuous actions accumulated in the past; it is like a field of barren soil that cannot be moistened by the downpour of rain.
And by the heat of passion, there is indeed no loss of the growth of crops. || 38 ||
One who knows the Self, subject to the ripening of prārabdha-karma and certain as to the ultimate limit [of his journey], does not suffer;
he is like a traveler on a road who knows the distance to the edge of the village.
Indeed, even when suffering, one does not despair midway on the path. || 39 ||
Perceiving both the internal and the external as the ultimate reality,
the steadfast man is not afflicted even when encountering intense calamity;
for he considers himself victorious at the very outset.
Even when overwhelmed by adversaries, one should not become despondent. || 40 ||
But worldly power, however supremely wonderful, does not delight one who is steadfast and has perceived its true nature;
just as a man whose body is adorned with the dress and ornaments of a woman [is not truly a man], despite his graceful charms.
Indeed, it is not even capable of deluding a wise youth. || 41 ||
Having realized the truth of his own inner self, hidden and uninterrupted within,
the wise man no longer indulges in sensual objects as he did before; he is like one who, by some stroke of fortune, has discovered a hidden treasure.
Why does he again assume the same wretchedness as before? || 42 ||
When one’s own majesty is firmly established, auspicious internal virtues spontaneously enter through the purification of conduct;
just as when a king has gained control over a loyal friend, his servants follow suit.
And these also, having approached him of their own accord, take refuge in him. || 43 ||

Ignorance itself does not exist; whence, then, could there be the contingency of the world? Even the discourse concerning the distinctions of the individual soul, the Lord, and the Teacher is far removed. [The reality] is the singular essence of consciousness, absolutely pure.
I am indeed Brahman alone, the all-pervading perfection. || 44 ||
Thus ends the *Advaitarasamañjarī*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Sadāśiva Brahmendra.
